title: Smile to brighten
purpose: Hear and feel how smiling while you speak changes your voice. The source says it can make a voice sound brighter and lighter.
instructions: Say a short everyday phrase the way you usually would.
Listen to both. Notice how smiling feels as well as how it sounds.
Through the day, try smiling a little more when you talk with people, and notice what changes.

primary_cue.text: Smile as you speak the phrase.

cues.text: Smile as you speak the phrase.
Smile a little more while you speak, then compare the two takes again.
Pay attention to how the smiling version feels as well as how it sounds.

practice_task.prompt_text: Black coffee, please. What are you up to today?

variants.label: Say it as you usually would

check_questions.text: Listen to both takes. Which sounds lighter and brighter to you?
How did smiling while speaking feel?

expected_observations: Smiling shortens the space between your voice box and your lips. The source says a smaller space means less “echo”, which can make a voice brighter and lighter.
common_misunderstandings: Lighter does not mean quieter, breathier or whispering.
What counts is how it sounds and feels to you. This is not a universal score.
stop_conditions: Stop the activity if you feel pain or discomfort, or notice unintended voice changes such as hoarseness. The source says this may mean you are going too quickly.
Take time to look after your voice, and try again when it feels better.
If problems persist or keep coming back, seek advice from a voice professional such as a speech and language therapist.
adaptations: Use phrases you actually say in daily life.
limitations: Public NHS patient-advice material written for self-guided practice. Lilt cannot check your technique, and it does not replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt does not measure lightness. Your own A/B listening is the evidence.
